# Gravitating Skyrmions and Baryon Stars: A Rational Map Approach

This study investigates the large baryon number sector of the Einstein-Skyrme model, examining its viability as a theoretical framework for modeling baryon stars—compact astrophysical objects that might be understood through the topological soliton solutions of nonlinear field theories coupled to gravity. The Skyrme model, originally proposed as a low-energy effective theory for baryons, provides solitonic solutions (skyrmions) characterized by an integer topological charge identified with baryon number. When coupled to general relativity, these solutions offer a potential avenue for constructing self-gravitating configurations that could serve as toy models for neutron stars or other compact baryonic matter.

Prior investigations into this problem focused primarily on the simplest ansatz for gravitating solitons: spherically symmetric "hedgehog" skyrmions, in which the field configuration maps radial directions in space directly onto directions in the internal isospin space. While this hedgehog ansatz has proven remarkably successful in flat-space Skyrme physics for describing single-baryon states, its extension to the gravitating case led to a discouraging conclusion. Energy analyses of these gravitationally coupled hedgehog configurations demonstrated that stable, bound multi-skyrmion stars could not be constructed within this framework—the energetic cost of maintaining spherical symmetry at large baryon number appeared to preclude the existence of stable solitonic stars altogether, casting doubt on the broader program of using Skyrme solitons to model compact astrophysical objects.

The present work departs from this restrictive hedgehog paradigm by introducing an alternative construction technique based on rational maps between Riemann spheres. This method, originally developed by Houghton, Manton, and Sutcliffe for flat-space multi-skyrmions, exploits the target space geometry of the Skyrme field to generate configurations with nontrivial angular structure, going beyond the simple radial symmetry of the hedgehog ansatz. By generalizing this rational map approach to the curved spacetime setting required for gravitational coupling, this paper constructs a new class of gravitating skyrmion solutions that were entirely inaccessible within the previous hedgehog-based framework.

Critically, this generalized construction succeeds in producing genuine multi-baryon bound states under gravity—precisely the stable, energetically favorable configurations whose existence had been ruled out by earlier hedgehog analyses. This result substantially revises the prospects for the Einstein-Skyrme model as a viable framework for baryon star physics, demonstrating that the previous no-go conclusions were an artifact of the restricted ansatz rather than a fundamental obstruction within the theory itself.

Remarkably, despite the manifestly non-spherical, angularly structured nature of the rational map construction at finite baryon number, the resulting solutions exhibit an emergent spherical symmetry in the large-$B$ limit. As the baryon number grows, the underlying polyhedral or shell-like arrangements characteristic of rational map skyrmions smooth out, and the energy density distribution approaches that of a spherically symmetric configuration. This recovery of spherical symmetry in the appropriate limit lends further physical credibility to the resulting solutions as candidates for macroscopic baryon stars, reconciling the microscopic angular structure of the rational map ansatz with the expected macroscopic symmetry of astrophysical compact objects.

# Gravitating Skyrmions and the Search for Baryon Stars

The Skyrme model, originally proposed as a low-energy effective theory for baryons arising from the low-energy limit of QCD, has long been recognized as a promising framework for describing compact, self-gravitating configurations of nuclear matter. When coupled to general relativity—yielding the so-called Einstein-Skyrme model—this theory admits soliton solutions that carry a conserved topological charge identified with baryon number, offering a natural candidate for modeling dense baryonic matter under strong gravitational fields, such as those found in neutron star interiors or hypothetical "baryon stars."

Previous investigations into gravitating skyrmions have predominantly relied on the spherically symmetric hedgehog ansatz, which restricts the Skyrme field configuration to a simple radial profile function multiplying a fixed angular dependence. While this ansatz is well-suited for describing the single-baryon sector (B=1) and has provided valuable insight into the interplay between the Skyrme field and spacetime curvature, its applicability to states with large baryon number is severely limited. In particular, prior studies employing this ansatz to explore multi-baryon states concluded that self-gravitating Skyrmionic configurations become energetically unfavorable for increasing baryon number, seemingly ruling out the existence of stable, macroscopic solitonic stars—an important negative result that cast doubt on the viability of the Einstein-Skyrme model as a realistic description of compact baryonic matter at astrophysical scales.

This study revisits the large baryon number sector of the Einstein-Skyrme model by employing a more sophisticated field configuration: the rational map ansatz. Unlike the hedgehog ansatz, which assumes a fixed, simple angular dependence, the rational map construction allows the Skyrme field to explore richer angular structures on the target sphere, parametrized by a rational map between Riemann spheres. This approach has proven highly successful in flat-space Skyrme model calculations, accurately capturing the shell-like and polyhedral symmetries observed in numerically exact multi-skyrmion solutions for a wide range of baryon numbers. By generalizing this ansatz to the curved-spacetime setting of the Einstein-Skyrme system, we construct gravitating multi-skyrmion configurations that more faithfully represent the true energy-minimizing field configurations at large B, moving beyond the overly restrictive hedgehog symmetry.

Our analysis demonstrates that when the rational map ansatz is properly incorporated into the gravitational sector, the resulting multi-baryon configurations exhibit markedly different energetic behavior compared to earlier hedgehog-based studies. Specifically, we find that stable, bound multi-baryon states persist and remain energetically favorable even at large baryon number, in direct contrast to the previous conclusion that stable solitonic stars were energetically excluded. This reversal arises because the rational map ansatz allows the Skyrme field configuration to adopt lower-energy, non-spherically-symmetric arrangements at intermediate baryon numbers—mirroring the polyhedral and shell structures familiar from flat-space multi-skyrmion physics—which more accurately capture the true ground-state energy landscape of the system when coupled to gravity.

Furthermore, we show that in the large-B limit, these multi-baryon configurations naturally recover an effective spherical symmetry, despite the intricate polyhedral or shell-like structures present at finite, moderate baryon numbers. This emergent spherical symmetry at large B provides a self-consistent link back to the hedgehog ansatz in the appropriate asymptotic regime, while correcting its shortcomings at finite and moderate values of B where the assumption of spherical symmetry is not justified. This finding is particularly significant for astrophysical applications, as it suggests that stable, self-gravitating Skyrmionic configurations—potential baryon stars—can indeed exist within the Einstein-Skyrme framework, provided that the internal field structure is allowed the freedom to explore the full space of topologically permissible configurations rather than being artificially constrained to spherical symmetry from the outset.

Taken together, these results substantially revise the prevailing understanding of the large baryon number sector of the Einstein-Skyrme model. By demonstrating that stable bound states exist and connect smoothly to a spherically symmetric limit at large B, this work reinstates the viability of solitonic baryon stars as a legitimate outcome of the Einstein-Skyrme model, opening new avenues for exploring the astrophysical implications of topological soliton models in the strong-gravity regime, including potential applications to neutron star equations of state, exotic compact objects, and the broader landscape of nontrivial topological structures in general relativistic settings.

# Gravitating Skyrmions and the Einstein-Skyrme System

## Introduction

The coupling of the Skyrme model to Einstein's theory of general relativity produces a rich framework for studying solitonic solutions in curved spacetime. This combined system, known as the Einstein-Skyrme system, has attracted significant attention in theoretical physics due to its implications for both particle physics and gravitational theory.

## The Skyrme Model

The Skyrme model, originally proposed by Tony Skyrme in the 1960s, describes baryons as topological solitons in a nonlinear theory of pions. The model is based on a Lagrangian containing a chiral field that maps spacetime into the group manifold SU(2). A crucial feature is the Skyrme term, a fourth-order derivative term that stabilizes the soliton solutions against collapse, in accordance with Derrick's theorem. These stable, particle-like solutions—called Skyrmions—carry a conserved topological charge identified with baryon number.

## Coupling to Gravity

When gravity is included, the Skyrme field acts as a source for the Einstein field equations, while the curved spacetime geometry influences the profile of the Skyrmion. This backreaction between matter and geometry gives rise to gravitating Skyrmions—self-gravitating solitonic configurations that solve the coupled Einstein-Skyrme equations simultaneously.

Key features of gravitating Skyrmion solutions include:

- **Self-gravitating solitons**: Unlike flat-space Skyrmions, these configurations account for the gravitational field generated by their own energy-momentum tensor.

- **Black hole hair**: The Einstein-Skyrme system admits solutions describing black holes with Skyrmion hair, challenging aspects of the no-hair conjecture. These solutions demonstrate that black holes can support nontrivial matter field configurations outside their horizons.

- **Stability and bifurcations**: As the coupling strength between gravity and matter increases, solution branches can bifurcate, giving rise to both stable and unstable configurations. Some solutions approach limiting cases resembling extremal black holes.

- **Multi-Skyrmion configurations**: Higher topological charge solutions correspond to multi-baryon states, with gravitational effects influencing their binding energies and geometric arrangements.

## Physical Significance

Gravitating Skyrmions serve as toy models for compact astrophysical objects, offering insights into how strongly interacting matter behaves under extreme gravitational conditions. They are relevant to:

- Neutron star physics, where dense nuclear matter may be modeled using Skyrmion crystals
- Early universe cosmology, where topological defects could have played a role in structure formation
- Mathematical physics, providing exact and numerical solutions that test analytical techniques in general relativity

## Mathematical Structure

The equations of motion for the Einstein-Skyrme system are derived by varying a combined action:

$$S = \int d^4x \sqrt{-g}\left[\frac{R}{16\pi G} + \mathcal{L}_{Skyrme}\right]$$

This yields the Einstein field equations sourced by the Skyrme energy-momentum tensor, alongside the Skyrme field equations modified by the curved background metric. Solving this coupled system typically requires numerical methods, particularly for spherically symmetric or axially symmetric ansätze.

## Conclusion

The Einstein-Skyrme system exemplifies the productive interplay between particle physics and general relativity. Gravitating Skyrmions provide a fascinating class of solutions that bridge topological soliton theory with strong-field gravity, offering theoretical laboratories for exploring fundamental questions about matter, spacetime, and the nature of compact objects in our universe.

We construct self-gravitating Skyrmion solutions using the rational map ansatz and investigate their properties as candidates for compact baryonic stars. By coupling the Skyrme model to general relativity, we obtain a family of static, spherically symmetric solutions labeled by baryon number *B*, constructed from degree-*B* rational maps between Riemann spheres. This approach allows us to efficiently generate high-charge Skyrmion configurations while preserving the discrete symmetries associated with Platonic solid arrangements of nucleons, extending previous flat-space multi-Skyrmion results into the strong-gravity regime.

We solve the coupled Einstein-Skyrme field equations numerically across a range of baryon numbers and gravitational coupling strengths, mapping out the mass-radius relations and compactness of the resulting solutions. As the coupling constant increases, the configurations undergo a transition from Skyrmion-like shell structures to increasingly compact, horizon-approaching states, with the maximum compactness approaching the Buchdahl bound. We identify critical coupling values beyond which stable solutions cease to exist, signaling gravitational collapse to a black hole, and we characterize the boundary between stable and unstable branches via a turning-point analysis of the mass as a function of central energy density.

Comparing energy densities and multipole structures across different *B* values, we find that higher baryon number solutions exhibit increasingly spherically symmetric energy distributions despite the polyhedral symmetry of the underlying rational map, consistent with a liquid-drop-like approach to uniform nuclear matter distributions at large *B*. We discuss the implications of these results for modeling dense baryonic matter, examining the extent to which topological soliton stars can mimic neutron star mass-radius relations, and outline extensions incorporating vector meson interactions and rotation for more realistic astrophysical comparisons.

# Einstein-Skyrme Model: Large Baryon Number Solutions

## Overview
This area of research investigates how gravitational coupling affects Skyrmion solutions (topological soliton solutions carrying baryon number) when embedded in a curved spacetime background, particularly examining what happens as the baryon number B becomes large.

## Key Findings

### 1. **Shell-like Structures at Moderate B**
For flat-space Skyrmions, minimal energy solutions at moderate baryon numbers typically organize into polyhedral or shell-like configurations (following patterns related to fullerene-like or crystalline arrangements) rather than spherically symmetric shapes. This reflects the discrete symmetry preferences of Skyrme solitons.

### 2. **Gravitational Effects Restore Spherical Symmetry**
A central result is that as gravitational coupling increases (or equivalently, as baryon number grows sufficiently large), the coupled Einstein-Skyrme system favors a **return to spherical symmetry**. This contrasts with the polyhedral symmetry breaking seen in ungravitated (flat-space) Skyrmion solutions. The self-gravity effectively smooths out the angular inhomogeneities that are energetically favorable in the absence of gravity.

### 3. **Stability Considerations**
- Spherically symmetric solutions in the Einstein-Skyrme model can become **stable** for large B, in contrast to flat space where such symmetric configurations are typically unstable saddle points relative to lower-symmetry deformations.
- The stability window depends on the interplay between the gravitational coupling constant and the Skyrme coupling parameters, with gravity providing a stabilizing influence against the shape-changing (symmetry-breaking) instabilities common in ungravitated Skyrmions.

### 4. **Connection to Compact/Dense Objects**
These solutions are often discussed in the context of:
- Boson-star-like compact objects supported by topological (Skyrmion) matter
- Analogues of neutron star interiors where high baryon density meets strong gravitational fields
- The existence of a critical baryon number or compactness threshold beyond which the spherical solution becomes the global energy minimum

### 5. **Existence of Solution Branches**
The large-B limit reveals branch structures analogous to those in other self-gravitating soliton systems (e.g., boson stars), including:
- A maximum mass/compactness for a given baryon number
- Possible bifurcation between stable and unstable spherical branches as functions of the gravitational coupling strength

## Physical Interpretation
The essential mechanism is that gravitational self-attraction increasingly dominates over the Skyrme field's internal (pionic) interactions as B grows, favoring the most efficient (spherically symmetric) packing of energy density, in analogy with how gravity enforces spherical symmetry in stars despite the underlying matter having no intrinsic preference for that shape.

# Abstract

We investigate the construction of gravitationally bound multi-baryon states within the Einstein-Skyrme framework using rational map ansätze, and demonstrate that this approach yields qualitatively distinct and more physically robust stability properties compared to the conventional hedgehog ansatz employed in earlier studies. While the hedgehog configuration, characterized by spherically symmetric field profiles, has been the traditional starting point for constructing self-gravitating Skyrmion solutions with baryon number B=1, its generalization to higher baryon number sectors suffers from significant limitations: the resulting energy densities fail to capture the shell-like and polyhedral symmetries known to minimize energy in flat-space multi-Skyrmion solutions, leading to configurations that are either dynamically unstable or require fine-tuned parameter regimes to achieve gravitational binding. In contrast, the rational map ansatz—which encodes the target-space topology through a holomorphic map between Riemann spheres—naturally incorporates the discrete symmetries associated with energy-minimizing Skyrmion solutions for B≥2, including tetrahedral, cubic, and icosahedral point group symmetries. We show that when coupled to gravity, these rational map configurations produce compact, self-gravitating multi-baryon solutions that remain stable across a substantially wider range of the gravitational coupling constant and Skyrme parameters than their hedgehog counterparts. Numerical solutions of the coupled Einstein-Skyrme field equations reveal that the rational map states exhibit lower total energy for fixed baryon number, smoother approach to the black hole formation limit, and the emergence of a critical compactness threshold beyond which stable branches connect continuously to the flat-space multi-Skyrmion limit. We further examine the role of higher baryon number sectors (B=2,3,4) in modifying the mass-radius relationship and the onset of gravitational collapse, finding that rational map solutions systematically postpone horizon formation relative to hedgehog-based configurations of equal baryon number. These results suggest that rational map ansätze provide a more reliable and physically motivated framework for modeling compact, topologically stabilized self-gravitating objects, with potential implications for exotic compact star models and the study of solitonic dark matter candidates supported by Skyrmion-like topological charge.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

Gravitating hedgehog skyrmion configurations have long been proposed as candidate models for self-gravitating solitonic stars, offering a topologically stabilized alternative to conventional stellar remnants. However, previous attempts to construct such solutions within the standard hedgehog ansatz have consistently failed to yield stable, physically viable stars at large baryon number. This shortcoming arises fundamentally from the rigid geometric structure imposed by the spherically symmetric hedgehog map, which couples the chiral field profile to the spatial coordinates in a manner that becomes energetically unfavorable as the soliton is compressed under self-gravity. As baryon number increases, the associated energy density grows without a corresponding mechanism to redistribute angular and radial stresses, leading to a runaway gravitational collapse or, alternatively, to solutions that violate the dominant energy condition or exhibit pathological curvature singularities before reaching astrophysically relevant compactness. Numerical continuation of these solutions reveals a maximum baryon number beyond which no static equilibrium exists, in sharp contrast to the behavior expected of genuine compact stars.

In this work, we introduce a generalized skyrmion ansatz that relaxes the strict hedgehog symmetry by incorporating an additional internal deformation degree of freedom, effectively decoupling the isospin orientation from the strict radial profile function. This modification introduces a new anisotropic stress contribution to the stress-energy tensor, which counteracts the collapsing tendency inherent to the standard construction. We demonstrate, both analytically in suitable limits and numerically via full solution of the coupled Einstein–Skyrme field equations, that this generalized configuration admits stable equilibrium branches extending to arbitrarily large baryon number. The resulting solitonic stars satisfy standard energy conditions, possess finite, regular geometry, and exhibit a mass–radius relation approaching a well-defined asymptotic scaling law characteristic of degenerate compact matter. These results establish, for the first time, a consistent gravitating skyrmion framework capable of describing macroscopic solitonic stars, and open new avenues for exploring topological solitons as viable dark compact objects or exotic neutron star alternatives.

# Abstract

We investigate the coupling of the Skyrme model to general relativity in the context of self-gravitating baryonic matter, focusing on equilibrium configurations across a wide range of baryon number B. Within the Einstein-Skyrme framework, soliton solutions—interpreted as baryon stars—are constructed by extremizing the total energy functional, comprising both the nonlinear sigma model/Skyrme term contributions and the gravitational binding energy, subject to a fixed topological charge constraint. We analyze the interplay between the short-range repulsive core inherent to the Skyrme term and the attractive gravitational interaction, demonstrating how this balance determines the mass-radius relationship and stability of the resulting configurations.

Particular attention is given to the large-B asymptotic regime, where we show that energy minimization strongly favors a transition from the complex, often multi-shell or crystalline arrangements characteristic of moderate baryon number to a single, spherically symmetric hedgehog-type configuration. We argue this emergent spherical symmetry arises because the surface-to-volume energy ratio associated with non-spherical or shell-like distributions becomes energetically prohibitive relative to gravitational compactification as B→∞, driving the system toward the maximally symmetric ansatz. We present numerical solutions of the coupled Einstein-Skyrme field equations in this limit, examining the resulting density profiles, compactness, and binding energy per baryon, and discuss the implications for the existence of a maximal mass and the onset of gravitational collapse. These results suggest that in the extreme baryon-number limit, the Einstein-Skyrme model admits stable, spherically symmetric baryonic star solutions whose bulk properties approach a well-defined continuum limit, offering insight into the behavior of dense topological solitonic matter under strong gravity.
